title: Prayer in the lab
hook: a careful study found no benefit from strangers praying for heart patients, and some believers say prayer isn't a lab tool (Benson et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday: honest placebo. Pills openly labeled as placebo still helped some patients, and your line was ritual helps. Where did a small ritual of care show up for you? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-two.

On a card: a first name and a last initial. That's all a small prayer group is handed. Somewhere else, a heart patient is waiting for bypass surgery, and the group has never met this person. They will pray for them anyway, as part of a study. Another group of patients gets no such prayers. A third group is told, for certain, that strangers are praying for them. Then the doctors count what happens after surgery. Today is about that study, what it found, and why people of faith and skeptics read the same result so differently.
screen: `A NAME ON A CARD.` → `STRANGERS PRAY, AS PART OF A STUDY.` → `THEN THE DOCTORS COUNT.`

segments.voice: First, the study. A team led by the cardiologist Herbert Benson followed patients having heart bypass surgery at several hospitals. Some were prayed for by groups from religious communities who knew only a first name and a last initial. Some were not prayed for by those groups. And some were told plainly that they were being prayed for. Second, the result. Prayer from strangers made no measurable difference to complications after surgery. And the patients who were told for certain that they were being prayed for had somewhat more complications, not fewer. The study offers no settled explanation for that. Third, how some believers answered. Some of them shrugged, and kept praying. Their point is older than any lab. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus is in the wilderness, and he is dared to throw himself down from the temple so that angels will catch him. In the King James words, he answers: "It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." To some readers, a controlled trial of God sounds a little like that dare: set up the test, then wait for heaven to perform. On this view, prayer is a relationship, not a dose of medicine. Fourth, how skeptics answered. For them the study is plain: if prayer from far away worked like a drug, a careful trial should catch it, and this one didn't. Both sides read the same paper. One says prayer isn't the kind of thing a lab can weigh. The other says the lab weighed it and found nothing. This path doesn't settle that argument. It asks you to hold both views with respect. Not a lab tool.
screen: `STRANGERS PRAYED FOR HEART PATIENTS.` · `NO MEASURABLE BENEFIT.` · `A TRIAL OF GOD AS A DARE?` · `THE SAME PAPER, TWO READINGS.` · then, large: `THOU SHALT NOT TEMPT THE LORD THY GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold two views at once. Settle, and let the breath slow. On an in-breath, bring up the first view: prayer is a relationship, and a lab can't weigh it. On the out-breath, bring up the second: a careful test looked, and found nothing. Don't pick a winner. Just let both sit in the room, the way two guests can share a couch. Notice whether either one tightens anything in you, and let it loosen. If you pray, you can pray now as you usually do. If you don't, stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Prayer in the lab. A careful trial found no benefit from strangers' prayers for heart patients, and some believers answer that prayer was never a lab tool. Today's word.
Your line: not a lab tool. Today, when you meet a view about faith you don't share, try stating it in its best form before you answer it. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: People of faith pray in many ways, for themselves and for others; some say prayer is a relationship with God rather than something a study can measure, while skeptics point to trials that found no effect.

fork.reveal: in Matthew, Jesus refuses the dare. some believers hear a controlled trial of prayer the same way: a test God isn't asked to pass.

original.note: Greek, from Matthew 4:7: "thou shalt tempt," in the sense of putting someone to the test.

trapdoor: what you thought: science proved prayer doesn't work.
what it means: one careful trial found no benefit from strangers praying for heart patients, and believers and skeptics read that result differently.
what a scholar hears: Benson's team tested intercessory prayer at a distance, by strangers, with patients split by what they were told; that is one kind of prayer, and the trial can only speak to it.

sources.ref: Benson et al., "Study of the Therapeutic Effects of Intercessory Prayer (STEP) in cardiac bypass patients" (American Heart Journal)

sources.quoted: It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God

notes: Confirm the STEP summary: coronary bypass patients at several hospitals; three groups (prayed for and uncertain, not prayed for and uncertain, prayed for and told for certain); prayer groups given first name and last initial; no difference in complications from prayer; the group told for certain had somewhat more complications. Percentages, patient counts and the year are deliberately left out.
Confirm Herbert Benson is fairly described as a cardiologist and as leading the study.
Confirm the Greek of Matthew 4:7 (οὐκ ἐκπειράσεις κύριον τὸν θεόν σου), the form ἐκπειράσεις, and the pronunciation given.
The church-hall scene in the hook is illustrative; the study's prayer groups came from religious communities, but the setting is not reported.
The reading of Matthew 4:7 as a reason not to test prayer experimentally is presented as some believers' view, not as the text's claim about science.
